unit.summary: Measure and adapt UIKit and SwiftUI interfaces, preserve list and editing identity, design interactions, and separate scene restoration from durable data in a source-backed UI lab.

lessons.title: Auto Layout: decide what grows, wraps, or shrinks
lessons.summary: Decide which view gets extra room and which gives up room. Keep text readable as the window, language, and text size change.
objectives: Explain a view's preferred size and the separate rules for growing and shrinking.
Build a title-and-badge row that stays readable in a narrow window and with larger text.
Choose the right layout guide for screen edges, text width, keyboard space, and scrolling.
Change the layout when its surroundings change without losing the current draft.

sections.title: Decide what happens when room runs out
sections.html:
Imagine fitting a name card and a small badge on one shelf. A longer name needs more room. The name can wrap, the badge can shrink, or the arrangement can change. Auto Layout is UIKit's system for solving rules about position and size together. Each constraint is one such rule. Start by choosing the outcome you want when space is scarce. An Android ConstraintLayout has a similar design problem, but iOS priorities are not Android layout_weight. Lesson 008 showed how to install constraints. Here we learn how to predict which rule gives way.

A constraint has the shape first attribute = multiplier × second attribute + constant, with a relation that can instead be less than or equal or greater than or equal. An anchor provides a typed way to create it. Leading and trailing express semantic reading directions; left and right express physical edges. Use the former for ordinary localized content. A height anchor cannot be equated with a leading anchor: typed anchors catch some nonsensical relationships before runtime, but cannot prove that the whole system is satisfiable.

Separate position from size and horizontal from vertical. For each axis ask what fixes the origin, what determines the extent, and which rule may yield. A label often supplies intrinsic size; an empty UIView usually does not. A row can therefore be fully determined without explicit width and height constants on every child. Conversely, adding more constraints does not necessarily remove ambiguity: redundant equalities can conflict while another dimension remains unconstrained. Draw the relationships and predict the result before opening the visual debugger.

sections.title: Growing and shrinking need different rules
sections.html:
Intrinsic content size means the size a view would prefer for its content. A label's text and font help determine it. Content hugging resists growing beyond that size. Compression resistance resists shrinking below it. These are separate choices for width and height. For preferred width w, think of hugging as width ≤ w and compression resistance as width ≥ w. Each preference has a priority, so another stronger rule can win. UIView.noIntrinsicMetric means the view supplies no preferred size on that axis. It does not mean the size must be zero.

A priority is a number that tells Auto Layout which preference to protect first. Required rules use 1000. Lower numbers are optional. Apple's guide gives common defaults of 250 for hugging and 750 for compression resistance, but inspect the actual control. If A hugs at 251 and B at 250, B is usually the first to grow when room is spare. If A resists compression at 751 and B at 750, B is usually the first to shrink when room is missing. Raising hugging does not raise compression resistance.

A practical arithmetic fixture makes the distinction observable. Suppose a row needs 180 points for its title, 60 for its badge, and 12 for spacing. At 300 points, 48 extra points must go somewhere; lower hugging identifies the expandable participant. At 220 points, 32 points must be recovered; lower compression identifies the participant allowed to shorten, unless wrapping changes the solution. Those numbers describe a synthetic model, not a measured device. Avoid equal competing priorities when the product requires a clear winner. Do not set every preference to required: incompatible required constraints produce a runtime conflict, not stronger accessibility.

sections.title: Let the title wrap and keep the badge readable
sections.html:
The row below has a long title and a short badge. The title can use several lines. The badge should keep its width for longer when space runs out. UIStackView arranges the two labels; the parent must give that stack a position and width. Neither label gets a fixed height. That leaves room for larger text. This example needs a scratch iOS target because it uses UIKit, Apple's framework for view and controller objects. It returns a view for a controller to place.

import UIKit

@MainActor
func makeDemoRow() -> UIView {
    let title = UILabel()
    title.text = "Demo provider with a deliberately long display name"
    title.numberOfLines = 0
    title.font = .preferredFont(forTextStyle: .body)
    title.adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true

    let badge = UILabel()
    badge.text = "Demo"
    badge.font = .preferredFont(forTextStyle: .caption1)
    badge.adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true
    badge.setContentHuggingPriority(UILayoutPriority(251), for: .horizontal)
    badge.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(UILayoutPriority(751), for: .horizontal)
    title.setContentCompressionResistancePriority(.defaultHigh, for: .horizontal)

    let row = UIStackView(arrangedSubviews: [title, badge])
    row.axis = .horizontal
    row.alignment = .top
    row.spacing = 12
    return row
}

The arrow declares the return type. UILayoutPriority(251) constructs the value expected by the setter; for: labels the axis argument. The leading dot on .horizontal abbreviates an enum case because the parameter type supplies context. numberOfLines = 0 removes the line-count cap. preferredFont selects a semantic text style, and adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory enables subsequent category updates. The stack creates arrangement constraints for its children; the caller must still determine the stack's position and available width.

Embed the row once, disable translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints on the externally constrained row, and connect its top and horizontal anchors to an appropriate guide. A multiline label's height depends on the resolved width. Re-measure after changing that width or text size; a screenshot at one width cannot certify it. This particular title is allowed to narrow and wrap while the badge resists narrowing. At extremely small widths even this policy may need a vertical arrangement or scroll container. Priority values cannot create physical space.

sections.title: Ask how tall the content needs to be
sections.html:
A preferred size and a fitted size answer different questions. Intrinsic content size is a view's input. systemLayoutSizeFitting asks what size the whole set of constraints needs. A self-sizing cell is a row whose height follows its content. Commonly, its width is fixed during measurement and its height is allowed to grow. Connect the contentView's top to its bottom through the content. A missing bottom constraint can leave height undecided. sizeToFit changes a frame directly; it cannot repair missing Auto Layout rules.

Invalidation means an old sizing answer needs to be checked again. Call invalidateIntrinsicContentSize when a custom view's content changes its preferred size. setNeedsLayout asks for a later layout pass. layoutIfNeeded performs pending layout now in the relevant hierarchy. Forcing layout while repeatedly changing sizing state can cause extra passes. Install constraints once. Keep a reference to a constraint whose constant must change, and replace a bounded set only when the structure changes.

For a UIScrollView form, contentLayoutGuide describes the scrollable content edges, while frameLayoutGuide describes the viewport. Constrain the content's four edges to the content guide, then match its width to the frame guide for vertical-only scrolling. Its internal vertical chain determines content height. Matching content height to viewport height as a required equality can unintentionally prevent scrolling. A long form needs a way to reach its last control at large text sizes; compressing every row until it fits is not that way. Session 033 adds keyboard-aware behavior to this geometry.

sections.title: Keep controls clear of covered edges
sections.html:
A safe area is the part of a view left clear by relevant system bars and container UI. Its insets are the gaps from the view's edges to that area. They can change as the screen changes. They are not fixed notch measurements or a complete keyboard rule. layoutMarginsGuide adds the container's chosen spacing. readableContentGuide keeps text from becoming too wide. A background may reach the outer edges while buttons stay inside a safe guide. Check which parent or child owns each gap before applying it twice.

For a form anchored above the keyboard, UIKit's keyboardLayoutGuide, available from iOS 15, provides layout relationships that track the keyboard. Its handling of an undocked keyboard is configurable; a floating iPad keyboard is not simply a full-width strip at the bottom. A scrolling form may instead combine keyboard-aware insets with scrolling the active field. Choose one avoidance owner and verify the full interaction. The guide does not select a text field, submit a value, or provide a Return key on a number pad.

The active address form's UIKit binding factory explicitly asks callers to establish child-controller containment and clears the hosting controller's safeAreaRegions for its particular scroll integration. That is an observed component contract, not a universal SwiftUI embedding recipe. A screen-level host often needs ordinary safe-area participation. When bridging, inspect the parent scroll view's adjustment behavior, the host's sizing options, and the child's safe-area policy together. A doubled bottom gap is usually a relationship problem, not evidence that every safe area should be ignored.

sections.title: Keep the draft when the window changes
sections.html:
Resizing means the available rectangle changes. It does not mean the user started a new draft. UIKit usually keeps the controller and views while adjusting their layout. Android can recreate an Activity for a configuration change, so that familiar habit is not a direct iOS rule. Keep the model and the current text-input owner unless the flow deliberately ends. A controller may be rebuilt for other reasons. Process termination, when the running app ends, is a separate question that needs a storage plan.

Trait collections describe environment dimensions such as horizontal size class, vertical size class, interface style, and preferred content-size category. Compact versus regular is a coarse classification, not a precise width, device model, or orientation. Two different widths can share the same class; an iPad window can become narrow without rotating the device. Use actual container geometry for continuous decisions, and relevant traits for semantic alternatives. Do not read UIScreen.main.bounds as the width of a particular scene or embedded child.

On iOS 17 and later, registerForTraitChanges can observe a specific set of trait definitions. Configure an initial state too: registration is for changes, not a promise of an initial callback. Earlier deployment support may require traitCollectionDidChange with relevant comparisons. viewWillTransition(to:with:) lets a controller coordinate size-transition work with UIKit's transition coordinator; layout callbacks can follow many times. Neither callback should refetch data just because geometry changed. Verify orientation support in the actual target and plist: production's inspected plist declares portrait on iPhone and four orientations on iPad. That configuration does not prove every feature adapts correctly.

sections.title: Read the sizing rules, then check the result
sections.html:
BookingTextField is a useful real example of intrinsic sizing: it tells its parent how much height the text needs. Changing usesCompactHeight invalidates that answer, meaning UIKit must ask again. The preferred text-size trait can also invalidate it. The view supplies no preferred width. Its height uses scaled font or design values. Text, editing, and placeholder rectangles are handled separately because they can need different line heights. A taller outer box alone may still clip the bottom of a letter. Inspect these rules before copying a helper into your own row.

AddressFormSectionView gives the error icon required horizontal hugging and compression resistance. Read that as a deliberate nonstretching icon decision, then examine whether the error label has enough width and unlimited lines. The infrastructure strictContentSize helper sets both preferences to required, while laxContentSize lowers both; these local conveniences are not neutral style helpers. Copying them onto a multiline label changes the failure policy. Use their implementation to understand the outcome before using their names.

For a broken layout, distinguish ambiguity, unsatisfiable constraints, and intentional truncation. Inspect hasAmbiguousLayout, use the view debugger, and add a symbolic breakpoint on UIViewAlertForUnsatisfiableConstraints in a scratch run. Give important constraints identifiers so diagnostics name the intended relationship. A conflict log often shows the constraint UIKit chose to break; that choice is not your product policy. Acceptance evidence should include narrow width, larger Dynamic Type, longer localized text, and visible final controls, plus an absence of unexpected conflict logs. Reading source alone does not establish those runtime results.

quiz.question: A title and badge must lose horizontal space. Which preference directly determines their resistance to shrinking?
options: Content hugging on the horizontal axis.
Content compression resistance on the horizontal axis.
The view's alpha.
quiz.explanation: Hugging resists expansion; compression resistance resists being smaller than the intrinsic extent. A lower compression priority yields first when competing optional preferences cannot all be satisfied.

quiz.question: A custom view returns UIView.noIntrinsicMetric for width. What does that mean?
options: Its width must be zero.
It ignores all horizontal constraints.
It supplies no intrinsic width; other constraints or the container must determine it.
quiz.explanation: The sentinel removes intrinsic sizing on that axis. It neither removes external constraints nor makes the view zero-sized.

quiz.question: An iPad window narrows without changing size class. What should the layout use?
options: Current container geometry for the width-dependent decision.
A guaranteed new controller created by rotation.
UIScreen.main.bounds as the width of every window.
quiz.explanation: Size class is coarse and may stay regular across multiple widths. iOS resizing usually preserves the existing hierarchy, and the physical screen need not match the scene or child width.

exercise.brief: In a separate UIKit scratch target, build the title-and-badge row. Change its width and text size, then explain which sizing rule wins.
steps: Install makeDemoRow once with top and horizontal constraints. Put a second row in a vertical scroll view with a complete content constraint chain.
Calculate the spare room at 300 points and missing room at 220 points before running the row.
Try long text, right-to-left layout, and accessibility text sizes. Use a vertical arrangement if the smallest supported width cannot fit the badge.
Inspect the installed constraints and any undecided layout. Record width, text size, and unexpected conflict messages.
Compare BookingTextField's height and placeholder rules with the ordinary UILabel row.
acceptance: The badge remains readable at the declared minimum supported width, or the documented alternative arrangement activates.
The title wraps without clipping and all scroll content remains reachable at accessibility sizes.
Constraints are installed once and there are no unexplained unsatisfiable-constraint logs.
The report distinguishes synthetic arithmetic, source evidence, and actual scratch observations.
exercise.solution:
Give the title a lower compression priority, the preference against shrinking, than the badge. The title then gives up width first and can wrap into extra height. Higher badge hugging resists giving spare width to the badge. The parent still needs to set the row's available width; otherwise these choices cannot predict the result. Install the row once in a scratch controller using the constraints below. At very small widths, choose the declared alternative arrangement rather than expecting priorities to create more room.

row.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
view.addSubview(row)
let guide = view.safeAreaLayoutGuide
NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
    row.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: guide.topAnchor, constant: 16),
    row.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: guide.leadingAnchor, constant: 16),
    row.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: guide.trailingAnchor, constant: -16)
])

This is a fragment inside a UIViewController method, not another standalone program. If the final content can exceed the viewport, use a scroll view rather than a required bottom equality that crushes the title. The arithmetic predicts a 32-point shortage at 220 points before wrapping; it is not a pixel-perfect prediction for a real font. The actual measurement must account for font metrics, text, and the layout's constraints.

A custom-height field also needs invalidation when its inputs change, as the repository example shows. Do not infer that a larger frame proves correct placeholder drawing. Record the largest text fixture and a keyboard-visible screenshot if appropriate. An unexecuted scratch run remains pending learner work; no production controller or baseline is changed by this solution.

I can distinguish intrinsic size from constrained fitting size.

simple.story: Mira has a shelf that is 300 centimetres wide. Her name card needs 180 centimetres, a badge needs 60, and the gap needs 12. That leaves 48 centimetres. She lets the name card use the spare room and keeps the badge neat. Later she moves both to a shelf only 220 centimetres wide. Now she needs to save 32 centimetres. She folds the name card onto another line before squeezing the badge. She has chosen both who may grow and who may shrink.
simple.meaning: Auto Layout uses priorities to make these choices in points. Hugging controls unwanted growth. Compression resistance controls unwanted shrinking. Wrapping can turn less width into more height.

example.before: A model row needs title 180 points + badge 60 points + gap 12 points = 252 points. The title has lower horizontal compression resistance than the badge.
example.change: Give the row 220 points of width while keeping the gap at 12 points.
example.after: The row is short by 32 points. In this simplified model, the title gives up width first. Its text may then need more height to wrap.

words.meaning: A rule relating a view's position or size to another value.
The size a view prefers from its content.
A preference against growing beyond the preferred size.
A preference against shrinking below the preferred size.
The region left clear by relevant system and container UI.

simple.remember: Choose who grows and who shrinks before choosing priority numbers.
simple.boundary: A shelf has only one width. Auto Layout solves many rules on two axes together. Real text size, wrapping, and required constraints can change the result; this arithmetic is not a device measurement.

lessons.title: Reusable lists: keep the right item in the right cell
lessons.summary: Keep each item's identity as rows move and cells are reused. Update changed text, reject old pages, and stop old images from appearing on new rows.
objectives: Tell apart an item ID, its current position, a cell object, and a cell reuse rule.
Build a list snapshot with unique IDs and refresh the content of items that stay.
Size list sections from the available window and keep selection tied to the item.
Load pages and prepare images with clear rules for duplicate work, cancellation, and old results.

sections.title: An item is more than its row number
sections.html:
Think of a reusable notice holder. Today it shows provider A; after scrolling, the same holder may show B. A cell is that reusable view object. Domain identity names the provider or displayed occurrence. IndexPath names its current section and position. A reuse identifier or CellRegistration tells UIKit which kind of cell to obtain and configure. These four names answer different questions. RecyclerView has similar reuse hazards, including an image arriving after its old row has gone. Start by separating the names so a moved item and a reused holder cannot be confused.

UITableView is primarily a vertically scrolling row interface; UICollectionView supports more general sections and layouts. Both reuse cells to bound the materialized hierarchy. Create permanent subviews in the cell's initializer or established setup hook, then apply complete content for the item being represented. If configure only sets an optional subtitle when nonempty, a later item without a subtitle can inherit the old text. Reset both presence and absence: set text, hidden state, accessories, callbacks, image placeholder, and accessibility content according to the current model.

Stable identity should survive content changes and reordering. Array offsets are therefore unsuitable identifiers for mutable lists. A label is unsuitable when localized or nonunique. A server provider ID may also be insufficient if the same provider legitimately appears twice in different sections: a displayed occurrence may need a composite ID. DiffUtil and stable RecyclerView IDs provide useful analogies, but UIKit's snapshot and reconfiguration contracts remain specific. Session 009's SwiftUI identity lesson becomes concrete here: the same record can move while retaining identity, and a cell object can represent entirely different records over time.

sections.title: Describe the list with stable IDs
sections.html:
A snapshot is a description of which list items exist and in what order. A diffable data source compares snapshots to update the list. It uses Hashable IDs: values with equality and a matching hash for lookup. Use an ID that stays the same when the subtitle changes. Keep display content in a separate store keyed by that ID. Using the whole mutable model as identity can turn an edit into a different item. Diffable APIs began in iOS 13; reconfigureItems began in iOS 15. Check the target's own minimum version, even though inspected production uses iOS 17.

An item ID must be unique across the whole snapshot. Add sections before their items. Editing a separate content dictionary does not itself tell the data source to configure surviving cells again. Mark changed surviving IDs with reconfigureItems. Use a suitable reload if the cell kind must change. Reconfiguration preserves the existing cell and does not call prepareForReuse, so configuration must also clear absent text, images, and actions. Newly inserted items already receive their first configuration.

Apply through one serialized UI owner so the content store and snapshot describe the same revision. Do not mix manual insert/delete calls with a diffable update for the same transition. An animation flag controls visual differences, not whether the underlying data is correct. A full reload can be appropriate for a deliberate wholesale reset, but destroys useful continuity if used after every keystroke. Empty, loading, and error states need explicit policies too; an empty snapshot cannot tell users whether no results were found or a request is still outstanding.

sections.title: Update the content, then update the snapshot
sections.html:
The helper below builds a snapshot from String item IDs. previousIDs means the IDs in the snapshot already shown by the data source. It does not mean any old page you happen to have saved. The caller still owns the collection view, the rule for configuring cells, the data source, and the content dictionary. This helper focuses on identity. It can be type-checked in a UIKit iOS 15 or later target; that check alone does not show a working list on a device.

import UIKit

enum DemoListSection: Hashable {
    case main
}

@MainActor
func makeDemoSnapshot(
    ids: [String],
    previousIDs: Set<String>
) -> NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<DemoListSection, String> {
    precondition(Set(ids).count == ids.count, "Duplicate demo IDs")
    var snapshot = NSDiffableDataSourceSnapshot<DemoListSection, String>()
    snapshot.appendSections([.main])
    snapshot.appendItems(ids, toSection: .main)
    let surviving = ids.filter { previousIDs.contains($0) }
    snapshot.reconfigureItems(surviving)
    return snapshot
}

Angle brackets supply generic arguments: the section enum and String item identifier. Set removes duplicates, so comparing counts checks uniqueness for this synthetic helper. precondition stops a programmer-invalid call; it is not user-facing validation or a good recovery policy for untrusted backend data. var is required because append and reconfigure mutate the snapshot value. $0 is the candidate ID in filter. This intentionally reconfigures all surviving items for simplicity; a larger list should determine which content actually changed.

At a render event, first publish the content for the new revision into the lookup store, then make and apply its snapshot on the owner's isolation context. In a cell provider, use the identifier argument supplied by the data source to look up content. For selection, resolve the current item identifier from the selected index path at the event boundary, then route by that ID. Capturing row number 3 when creating a callback can select a different record after insertion. The callback should either capture immutable identity or perform a current lookup, according to the feature contract.

sections.title: Check who an image belongs to before showing it
sections.html:
Reuse means a cell object gets a new job. prepareForReuse is a hook before a dequeued cell is used for another item. Call super and clear work that belongs to that cell. Reconfiguration can skip this hook, so each configuration must set complete content. Store the current representedID and the image task handle. When an image finishes, check the current ID before showing it on the UI actor, which protects UI-state access. Cancellation is a request, not instant stopping. An old task can still finish, so the ID check remains necessary.

If an image request is shared by a cache or loader, cancelling one cell's interest should not cancel data needed by another visible cell. A loader can deduplicate by a resource key and manage separate consumer interests. Reset the placeholder when configuration changes; otherwise an old image remains visible while the new request waits. Downsampling and decoding are performance-specialist topics developed in the performance unit. Here the essential acceptance criterion is correctness: after rapid scrolling and reordering, every visible card must show the content associated with its current ID.

Callbacks also count as reusable content. Replace the old action during every configuration and avoid installing another target or gesture recognizer each time. A retained closure can keep an obsolete model or owner alive, even when the displayed text is fresh. Accessibility labels, values, selected states, and custom actions must likewise match the represented item. UIKit's cell highlight and selection styling are interaction state; do not accidentally persist them as the business selection. A row selected for a detail route and a checkbox toggled in a draft often need different state owners.

sections.title: Build section sizes from items and groups
sections.html:
A compositional layout describes a collection in pieces: items form groups, and groups form sections. A fractional size takes a share of its containing dimension. An absolute size is a fixed number of points. An estimated size is an initial guess that content measurement can replace. A height estimate does not fix broken constraints inside a cell. Let both item and group sizing support text that grows vertically. A height that fits a short English label may clip a longer translation or larger text.

Orthogonal scrolling lets a section scroll along an axis independent of the main collection's direction, such as a horizontal carousel in a vertical page. groupPagingCentered describes that section's paging behavior; it is not a blanket pagination API. A section provider receives a layout environment with effective container geometry. Choose one or two columns from that geometry rather than the physical screen width. Insets and inter-item spacing must be included in the width budget. Stable item IDs continue to matter when a width change rearranges columns.

Table rows need the equivalent complete sizing contract: automaticDimension, a useful estimated row height, and constraints from contentView's top through all required children to its bottom. Estimates help initial scroll geometry, but large systematic errors can cause visible jumps. Avoid nesting an unconstrained scrolling list inside another scroll view merely to make content height automatic. The active carousel uses a custom grow-only intrinsic-height floor to bootstrap an estimated orthogonal layout. That narrowly documented compromise leaves trailing whitespace after shorter content and should not become a universal list-sizing recipe.

sections.title: Loading another page differs from preparing an image
sections.html:
Pagination loads another logical page of items. Prefetch gets resources ready for items that may soon appear. UICollectionViewDataSourcePrefetching gives current index paths; translate them to current IDs when the callback arrives. The prediction may be cancelled or never happen. Cell configuration must still load required content if nothing was prefetched. Keep one owner for a page request and a separate interest for a thumbnail. Otherwise a reused cell can accidentally control list-wide work, or every predicted row can start the same page again.

Give each query a generation number, each page a cursor, and each active load a saved generation-and-cursor pair. Keep ordered IDs and an explicit end state. A near-end callback starts a page only if that pair is not already loading. Choose what duplicate IDs mean: for example, update stored content without adding another occurrence. Define what to do with a repeated cursor or an empty page that still claims more data. On retry, keep useful rows and show that only the additional page failed.

When a query changes, increment its generation, clear or deliberately retain old presentation according to the product policy, and reject old results in both success and failure paths. If page B can finish before page A, either serialize cursor-based loads or buffer results with an explicit ordering rule. Actor isolation alone does not make arrival order equal page order. Keep requests in the feature model or service owner, not arbitrary recycled cells. A page affects the list; a thumbnail request affects one resource interest. Record these owners separately when debugging scrolling stalls or wrong results.

This minimal synchronous commit seam makes the old-success and old-error schedules concrete. It serializes one page per current query; transport, next-cursor discovery, content updates, and cancellation classification remain with the surrounding owner:

struct PageTicket: Equatable {
    let generation: Int
    let cursor: String
}

@MainActor
final class PageCommitOwner {
    private var generation = 0
    private var inFlight: PageTicket?
    private(set) var ids: [String] = []
    private(set) var failed = false

    func replaceQuery() {
        generation += 1
        inFlight = nil
        ids = []
        failed = false
    }
    func begin(cursor: String) -> PageTicket? {
        guard inFlight == nil else { return nil }
        let ticket = PageTicket(generation: generation, cursor: cursor)
        inFlight = ticket
        return ticket
    }
    func complete(_ result: Result<[String], Error>, ticket: PageTicket) {
        guard ticket.generation == generation, inFlight == ticket else { return }
        inFlight = nil
        switch result {
        case .success(let page):
            var seen = Set(ids)
            ids += page.filter { seen.insert($0).inserted }
            failed = false
        case .failure:
            failed = true
        }
    }
}

Begin A/p1 and keep its ticket. Replace the query, begin B/p1, complete B successfully with [“B”], then complete A once with success and, in a fresh replay of the schedule, with an ordinary failure. In both cases IDs stay [“B”] and failed stays false. Before completing B, completing A must also leave B’s in-flight ticket intact; a duplicate begin remains nil. Expected values are independent of response order. The generation distinguishes identical cursors across queries. This seam drops duplicate IDs with first-occurrence order; a real content store must separately apply its agreed update policy.

sections.title: Read what the current carousel actually does
sections.html:
CareTeamCarousel is the reusable card list in the active Projects source. PracticeViewController chooses it behind iOS_PracticePageQuerySplit, a feature gate that selects a code path. The alternative still uses ProfessionalCarousel. The comments explain why reusable cards were introduced, but they do not show measured speed or prove that every user receives the new branch. Read the ID lookup, update rules, and gate as source evidence. A scrolling or launch claim needs a separate run with recorded conditions.

The diffable data source uses ProfessionalId, while modelsById resolves current card content. Tap handling resolves that ID again rather than retaining a row position. display collapses both the title's arranged wrapper and the collection for an empty model before its unchanged guard; otherwise the first empty update would leave an unwanted blank band. It skips equivalent model updates, reconfigures persisting IDs, rebuilds layout when crossing the single-versus-many boundary, and crossfades particular reorders. Each decision solves a concrete state or geometry contract, not an abstract instruction to animate every snapshot.

The shared RedisplayableCollectionViewCell forwards prepareForReuse to its reusable subview. Compare that generic hook with the carousel's complete configure method: reconfiguration still needs correct content when reuse cleanup does not run. For audit evidence, record the ID sequence, selected ID, configuration count, and outstanding resource interests under a controlled fixture. Source reading can establish the guard and lookup design; only a scratch or authorized client run can establish runtime correctness and cost. Instruments work, representative devices, and frame distributions belong to the performance unit. Avoid converting a recycling comment into a fabricated benchmark.

quiz.question: A diffable item keeps its ID but its subtitle changes. What is the reliable update policy?

lessons.title: SwiftUI layout: ask for a size, then place the view
lessons.summary: Follow how SwiftUI asks children for sizes and places them. Predict modifier order, build reusable view descriptions, and check custom layout and geometry reports.
objectives: Explain proposed size, child size, and placement, including missing and unlimited proposed dimensions.
Predict how modifier order changes spacing, drawing, and touch regions.

Send size information up the view tree without causing repeated layout changes.

sections.title: The parent asks; the child answers
sections.html:
A size proposal is a parent's question: how much room would you use here? The child reports its answer, then the parent places it. SwiftUI's ProposedViewSize carries that question. It is not a hard promise that every child fits exactly. Compose also separates measurement from placement, but its constraints have different rules. SwiftUI can ask a child several times with different proposals. Measuring is therefore not a one-time lifecycle event. Do not start a request or save screen state merely because a sizing method was called.

Each proposed dimension can be absent. nil means unspecified: ask for the child's ideal size on that axis. Zero asks about its minimum behavior. Infinity asks about its maximum behavior. They are different questions. Treating nil as zero can collapse content that needs its ideal width. A custom layout must still return a meaningful finite concrete size. State what it does for each probe and for no children before treating a normal-width screenshot as proof.

Text responds differently when width is constrained because line wrapping changes height. A vertical ScrollView commonly gives its content an unspecified proposal on the scrolling axis rather than a fixed viewport height. A GeometryReader tends to occupy available proposed space, so placing one as the main child of a small row can alter the row's size instead of merely observing it. A view's semantic font and localization are inputs to this negotiation. The lesson's measurements use synthetic views; the active repository's layout math supplies useful source evidence, not a claim that every SwiftUI child follows identical fitting behavior.

sections.title: Read wrappers from the inside out
sections.html:
A modifier wraps an existing view description with another description. Order matters. Text("Demo").padding(12).background(.yellow) adds spacing first, so yellow covers the padded area. Text("Demo").background(.yellow).padding(12) adds the spacing outside yellow. Read from the Text outward to see which size each wrapper receives. These expressions do not keep changing one durable Android View object. They build values that describe the UI. A change that looks cosmetic can therefore also change measured size and where the result is drawn.

frame adds a size-and-alignment wrapper; it does not directly assign the child's UIKit frame. The child can still draw outside it. clipped hides drawing outside the clipping region, but does not repair unreadable content or create a larger touch target. offset moves the drawing without giving neighboring views new layout space. padding changes measured space. When views overlap, first identify which operation changed size and which only changed drawing.

fixedSize asks a view to preserve ideal behavior along chosen axes. fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true) can help text use required vertical extent while negotiating width, but it is not a universal clipping remedy and can exceed a fixed-height ancestor. layoutPriority influences how a container allocates space among children; it is not a direct equivalent of Auto Layout's separate hugging and compression inequalities. HStack, VStack, Spacer, overlays, and backgrounds have different layout participation. For an overlay badge, ask whether the badge should determine the parent's size or merely decorate it. Also inspect contentShape and control semantics before assuming the drawn rectangle is the hit target.

sections.title: Build several views into one description
sections.html:
some View means the caller does not need to spell out the exact returned view type. The compiler still knows it. ViewBuilder is a result builder: it turns several view expressions and supported branches into one typed composition. It does not create a runtime bag of unrelated view objects. An ordinary some View function cannot freely return Text in one branch and Button in another unless their result is unified by a builder or another structure. The builder records those alternatives in the resulting type.

import SwiftUI

struct DemoPanel<Content: View>: View {
    private let content: Content

    init(@ViewBuilder content: () -> Content) {
        self.content = content()
    }

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 8) {
            content
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

struct BuilderDemo: View {
    let showHint: Bool

    var body: some View {
        DemoPanel {
            Text("Demo form")
            if showHint {
                Text("The hint is optional")
            }
        }
    }
}

Content: View constrains the generic type parameter. () -> Content is a zero-argument closure returning that content. The trailing closure in DemoPanel { ... } supplies it. The builder annotation belongs to the initializer parameter, so the caller can write several expressions. The initializer evaluates the closure and stores its resulting description; this version does not store an escaping closure or run work on later events.

Conditional structure also influences identity. Switching unrelated branches can replace local state; a consistent tree with changing inputs often preserves it. AnyView erases a concrete type when a boundary needs that flexibility, but adding type erasure everywhere does not solve poor identity or ownership. For repeated data use ForEach with stable IDs, not a language-level for loop that performs arbitrary mutations inside body. Keep side effects in actions or defined lifetime hooks, and treat builder errors as type/structure problems before blaming rendering.

sections.title: Give a custom layout clear size rules
sections.html:
The Layout protocol lets you write SwiftUI's measurement and placement rules from iOS 16 onward. A protocol states the methods your type must provide. These methods receive subview proxies, handles for asking about and placing children. They are not mutable UIKit views. DemoColumn stacks children vertically. It uses a finite proposed width, or the widest child's ideal width when no finite width is supplied. Children get no proposed height. A child may refuse the width and overflow; that is an explicit limit of this example.

import SwiftUI

struct DemoColumn: Layout {
    var spacing: CGFloat = 8

    private func width(for proposal: ProposedViewSize, subviews: Subviews) -> CGFloat {
        if let width = proposal.width, width.isFinite {
            return max(0, width)
        }
        return subviews.map { $0.sizeThatFits(.unspecified).width }.max() ?? 0
    }

    func sizeThatFits(
        proposal: ProposedViewSize,
        subviews: Subviews,
        cache: inout Void
    ) -> CGSize {
        guard !subviews.isEmpty else { return .zero }
        let width = width(for: proposal, subviews: subviews)
        let childProposal = ProposedViewSize(width: width, height: nil)
        let heights = subviews.map { $0.sizeThatFits(childProposal).height }
        let gaps = max(0, spacing) * CGFloat(subviews.count - 1)
        return CGSize(width: width, height: heights.reduce(0, +) + gaps)
    }

    func placeSubviews(
        in bounds: CGRect,
        proposal: ProposedViewSize,
        subviews: Subviews,
        cache: inout Void
    ) {
        let childProposal = ProposedViewSize(width: bounds.width, height: nil)
        var y = bounds.minY
        for child in subviews {
            let size = child.sizeThatFits(childProposal)
            child.place(at: CGPoint(x: bounds.minX, y: y),
                        anchor: .topLeading, proposal: childProposal)
            y += size.height + max(0, spacing)
        }
    }
}

inout Void satisfies the protocol's cache parameter without storing a cache. guard handles empty content before subtracting one from its count. reduce(0, +) sums heights using the addition operator as a function. bounds.minX and bounds.minY preserve a nonzero assigned origin. Child placement receives the same width policy used during measurement of the assigned bounds. Assume child responses are finite, as valid layout responses should be; do not conceal malformed children with an arbitrary giant fallback size.

This layout deliberately ignores a proposed height and reports the height its content needs. A fixed-height ancestor may therefore require scrolling or a separate compact design. It also omits baseline alignment, RTL-specific ordering, and caching optimization. State those limits when reviewing it. A valid narrow contract is more useful than an unexplained imitation of VStack whose behavior differs in edge cases.

sections.title: Reuse a size answer only while its inputs match
sections.html:
A layout cache keeps answers from earlier work so you may reuse them. An old answer is useful only if its inputs still match. Child text, fonts, count, width, spacing, and environment can change the arrangement. makeCache and updateCache handle the protocol's cache lifecycle, but width-dependent answers still need a suitable key or fresh calculation. Do not save the last measured size by changing observed screen state inside measurement. The parent may ask again, and that state change can ask for yet another layout pass.

The active FlowLayout measures each child with .unspecified, calls pure arrange math with proposal.width, and recomputes arrangement for bounds.width during placement. It adds the assigned bounds origin before placing children. Its documented rows align to the widest row, not automatically the outer container. Thus an external frame alignment is a separate choice. A pill wider than the line budget is placed and allowed to overflow; that is a source-defined policy you should verify against the intended content, not label as universally responsive.

The pure arrangement tests cover empty input, one item, wrapping, oversize children, distributions, and vertical alignment. Read those assertions to discover the contract, then separately ask whether the SwiftUI subviews provide appropriate measurements. Ideal-size measurement of every child may be suitable for short chips but needs investigation for long multiline content at accessibility sizes. Algorithm tests do not exercise the text renderer or input environment. The accompanying snapshot tests add another boundary of evidence, but their source presence does not mean they were run in this audit.

sections.title: Send geometry up with a clear combining rule
sections.html:
A preference lets a child report information up to an ancestor. Environment values usually travel down. PreferenceKey describes the reported value, its default, and how several reports combine. reduce(value:nextValue:) performs that combination. inout lets it change the current combined value. Calling nextValue() obtains the next child's report. If children report heights 20 and 40, overwriting gives 40 for that order; taking the maximum gives 40 regardless of that order. Collecting heights by stable ID answers a different question again.

Use GeometryReader in a background or overlay when you intend to observe an existing view's assigned size without making the reader the principal sizing child. Choose a named coordinate space when positions should be relative to a particular scrolling container. A global y coordinate and a local viewport height cannot be subtracted meaningfully just because both are CGFloat. Remember that geometry can change after a keyboard, safe-area, content, or window transition even when the data model stays the same.

The active AI chat reports a zero-height bottom marker's position in the named aiChatScroll coordinate space. Its preference key overwrites because that marker is the intended single contributor. Introducing multiple emitters without changing reduction would silently change the meaning. The receiver updates bottom-marker state to decide whether a scroll control appears. Guard no-op changes and avoid a loop where the displayed control changes geometry, which changes the preference, which toggles the control again. Prefer directly deriving layout inside Layout where possible; use stateful geometry reporting for an actual interaction need, not to reproduce every child's frame as model data.

sections.title: Agree on size at the UIKit boundary
sections.html:
A bridge lets UIKit content appear in SwiftUI, or SwiftUI content appear in UIKit. Each side still has its own sizing rules. A represented UIKit view can answer SwiftUI proposals through sizeThatFits(_:uiView:context:) from iOS 16. Returning nil asks for the framework's default strategy. Returning a concrete size makes your own measurement policy responsible. Measure a multiline label at the intended width. Its preferred size before layout may answer a different question. updateUIView applies new inputs; measuring must not also report a user edit.

For SwiftUI content hosted in UIKit, UIHostingController sizingOptions can request intrinsicContentSize or preferredContentSize updates, with the relevant iOS 16-era availability. Those values serve different parent-container contracts. Setting both does not replace parent constraints, containment, or a scroll policy. The repository's wrappers add their own resizing behavior, so inspect the actual helper rather than assuming it is an unmodified Apple host. Ordinary UIKit constraints surrounding a host and SwiftUI proposals inside it can both be correct while disagreeing at their boundary.

A useful acceptance record identifies finite, unspecified, zero, and wide-width proposals; empty content; a nonzero placement origin; larger text; and an RTL fixture. First type-check a scratch example against its declared deployment version. Then exercise actual layout; a compiler does not prove measured sizes. Record whether bounds exceed the reported extent and whether that is the declared overflow policy. Special topics such as baseline guides, layout-value keys, right-to-left custom placement, and complex cache optimization need additional focused practice beyond this introductory custom layout.

lessons.title: Interaction: keep state, movement, scrolling, and focus in agreement
lessons.summary: Make the final state correct before animating it. Handle interrupted drags, scroll to current item IDs, and give each input field one clear focus name.
objectives: Tell apart a state change, animated movement, insertion or removal, and the update that carries animation settings.
Separate movement during a drag from the saved position, and provide another way to do essential actions.
Scroll to stable IDs using the reader that belongs to the current content.
Give each field a unique focus value and decide what dismissal should do.
Choose checks for interrupted movement, keyboard use, reduced motion, and cancelled navigation.

sections.title: Choose the right final state first
sections.html:
State is the value describing what the interface should show. Animation fills in eligible visual steps between old and new values. When expanded changes from false to true, the detail belongs in the new state immediately, even while its appearance moves or fades. SwiftUI's withAnimation attaches animation information to a synchronous state change. It does not wait for the pixels to finish before changing the value. Compose offers a useful starting idea, but the exact runtime rules differ. A network result still needs a current-result check even if the list fades into view.

Interpolation changes an eligible value while the view keeps its identity, such as moving from one opacity to another. A transition describes a child entering or leaving the tree. A permanently present child does not enter just because it has .transition(.opacity). Replacing identity can remove local state instead of smoothly changing the old view. Decide whether the action changes a property, adds or removes a child, or replaces a whole flow before choosing the visual effect.

The Android analogy breaks at exact modifier and runtime contracts. SwiftUI's .animation(_:value:) watches the supplied Equatable value and applies animation within its subtree when that value changes; other simultaneous changes in that scope can inherit the same transaction. A broad animation modifier can therefore animate unrelated error, keyboard, or layout updates. Place scope deliberately, and do not use animation duration as a synchronization primitive for data or navigation. A visual completion is not the same as exactly-once selection-result delivery.

sections.title: Keep animation settings near the change
sections.html:
A transaction carries information for one update, including its animation. withTransaction supplies that information for a state change. A .transaction modifier adjusts it in part of the view tree. nil animation requests no animation in that setting; disablesAnimations also prevents ordinary animation modifiers from adding one to that transaction. Those choices have related but different effects. The disclosure below reads reduced motion, a system preference for less movement, and keeps the same final expanded state under either policy.

import SwiftUI

struct DemoDisclosure: View {
    @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion
    @State private var expanded = false

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading) {
            Button(expanded ? "Hide demo details" : "Show demo details") {
                withAnimation(reduceMotion ? nil : .easeInOut(duration: 0.2)) {
                    expanded.toggle()
                }
            }
            .accessibilityValue(expanded ? "Expanded" : "Collapsed")

            if expanded {
                Text("Synthetic details remain readable without motion.")
                    .transition(.opacity)
            }
        }
    }
}

The backslash key path identifies the environment value. The conditional expression chooses no explicit animation when reduced motion is enabled. expanded.toggle() changes the final state immediately; SwiftUI handles eligible visual interpolation. The if makes the detail enter or leave the tree, so its transition applies to an actual insertion/removal. The button supplies a semantic action and reports its expanded state to accessibility rather than relying on an unexplained tap gesture.

Reduced motion is a product policy, not necessarily a demand to eliminate all feedback. A subdued fade or immediate update may communicate the same outcome without large movement. Check VoiceOver order after insertion, large text expansion, and repeated taps during interpolation. The final visible state must correspond to the final Boolean even if an earlier animation was interrupted. Do not leave an invisible interactive overlay intercepting touches after a transition.

sections.title: Lay out the start before animating the end
sections.html:
UIKit animates eligible property changes inside UIView.animate, such as opacity or a new layout position. For a changing constraint, first lay out the starting state in the ancestor that owns the relationship. Change the constant, then call layoutIfNeeded on that hierarchy inside the animation block. This gives UIKit both the starting and ending layout. Calling it only on the child can miss a parent-owned change. Direct frame changes can also snap back when Auto Layout calculates its own answer again.

UIViewPropertyAnimator offers explicit start, pause, continuation, reversal, and fraction-complete controls for interruptible interactions. Know the difference between its current visual position and the model's intended final state. A user can reverse or cancel an interactive transition; do not commit a domain operation solely because an animation started. Navigation container transitions have their own coordinators and cancellation information. Session 010's exactly-once result policy still needs a terminal event that represents the actual outcome.

The active care-team carousel uses a cross-dissolve around a nonanimated snapshot apply, followed by layoutIfNeeded, because its implementation documents unreliable per-cell moves in that orthogonal layout. This is a narrowly chosen implementation, not advice that all diffable lists should crossfade. It skips equivalent state and treats initial population differently from a reorder. No timing measurement was performed in this course audit. If replacing that strategy, specify the visual requirement and compare actual interrupted interactions on representative environments before claiming an improvement.

sections.title: Keep a drag's temporary movement separate
sections.html:
A gesture is a recognized pattern of input, such as a drag. Use a standard Button for ordinary activation. @GestureState holds temporary gesture data and resets when the gesture ends or is cancelled. @State can hold the saved position. Translation means movement since this drag began. If the saved x position is 10 and translation reaches 5, display 15. When translation later reaches 8, display 18, not 23. Add the current translation to the saved origin for display, then save once when the drag ends successfully.

import SwiftUI

struct DemoDrag: View {
    @State private var savedOffset = CGSize.zero
    @GestureState private var translation = CGSize.zero

    var body: some View {
        Text("Demo draggable label")
            .padding()
            .background(.thinMaterial)
            .offset(x: savedOffset.width + translation.width,
                    y: savedOffset.height + translation.height)
            .gesture(
                DragGesture(minimumDistance: 10)
                    .updating($translation) { value, state, _ in
                        state = value.translation
                    }
                    .onEnded { value in
                        savedOffset.width += value.translation.width
                        savedOffset.height += value.translation.height
                    }
            )
            .accessibilityAction(named: Text("Reset demo position")) {
                savedOffset = .zero
            }
    }
}

updating receives the gesture value, an inout transient state, and transaction; the underscore discards the unused transaction. The code is a syntax and lifetime demonstration, not a complete bounded draggable component. It lacks edge clamping and keyboard directional controls. Add those for a real movable item, and ensure every essential operation has a non-drag route.

Gesture composition matters inside a scroll view. simultaneousGesture allows recognition alongside another gesture; highPriorityGesture changes precedence. Neither is a universal fix for conflicts. A broad drag on a row can steal scrolling or back navigation, and a zero minimum distance can turn ordinary taps into drags. Specify the recognized direction, target region, cancellation behavior, and accessible alternative, then observe actual interaction rather than assuming modifier order settles every recognizer conflict.

sections.title: Scroll to a current ID with a current reader
sections.html:
A scroll target is the ID of content you want to bring into view. ScrollViewReader supplies a proxy, a handle whose scrollTo method requests that movement in its contained scroll view. The intended ID must still exist there. An accessibilityIdentifier names content for automation and is a separate mechanism. Old array positions can point to different rows after insertion. New random IDs created during body evaluation can disappear before the scroll request arrives. Use stable item identity, as in lesson 030, and keep the reader near the event.

Keep the proxy near the event that uses it. Capturing a proxy in a closure stored during onAppear can leave a stale layout context when content collapses, expands, or the hierarchy changes without another appearance event. The active AI chat observes its scroll request subject inside ScrollViewReader and calls the current proxy there. Its source comment documents a full/text-entry-only/full resize problem in the former captured-closure strategy. That is checked implementation evidence; the course has not reproduced the original runtime bug.

Do not auto-scroll to the bottom after every incoming item if the user intentionally scrolled upward. Define whether the viewport was near the bottom before insertion, whether this message was the user's own submission, and whether a visible New messages action should appear. A zero-height stable bottom marker can be a valid target. Newer scroll-position and target-layout APIs beginning in iOS 17 provide additional control, but do not retroactively appear in every repository component. Verify availability, target placement, and identity before adopting them. Programmatic scrolling also needs a reduced-motion policy and must not fight interactive keyboard dismissal.

sections.title: Give each field one focus name
sections.html:
Focus names the control that should receive input. @FocusState connects SwiftUI focus to a Boolean or optional Hashable value. For several fields, use an optional enum with one case per field. .name identifies the name field; nil means no field should be focused. Apply .focused to the actual control. Giving two controls the same case makes a programmatic request ambiguous. Keep one clear owner for this rule even if a view model also carries requests related to validation or navigation.

UIKit's becomeFirstResponder asks a control to accept input focus and returns whether it accepted. A field not yet in the presented hierarchy may not show a keyboard. An early SwiftUI focus assignment is also a request, not proof of visible keyboard input. A scheduled task or a delay does not establish a specific lifecycle milestone. Inspect an actual deferral's guard and runtime result before copying it as a general focus rule.

Keyboard visibility, text-input focus, and VoiceOver accessibility focus are separate. A hardware keyboard can edit a focused field without a software keyboard, and moving VoiceOver to an error is not necessarily the same as making that text field first responder. Session 033 uses focus for submit progression and error recovery. During a sheet dismissal or a navigation return, decide whether focus should resume, remain cleared, or move to an invalid field. Avoid resetting all form state to gain focus: that sacrifices editing identity and can erase an unsaved draft.

sections.title: Record events as well as the final picture
sections.html:
An event record lists what changed and when. Record state changes, navigation outcomes, focus requests, accepted input-focus changes, and scroll requests. These events can occur in a different order from visible animation. Try repeated disclosure taps, a cancelled drag, a cancelled back gesture, scrolling with the keyboard open, and a scroll request after resizing. A screenshot shows one final picture. It cannot establish whether a cancelled gesture preserved the draft or whether an action delivered its result exactly once.

Preserve semantic controls. Button supports activation and accessibility behavior that a Text with onTapGesture does not automatically reproduce. A custom drag should expose an alternative action, suitable hit region, and a meaningful accessibility value. Make decorative overlays ignore hit testing when appropriate. Verify larger text does not cover another control, and test reduced motion with the same final content and actions. A hover or keyboard shortcut may help iPad interaction, but declaring iPad support alone does not prove pointer, focus traversal, or external-keyboard quality.

The active BookingAddressFormView has one optional field FocusState and maps submit events through its field enum. CreatePatientView mirrors model/view focus and requests initial focus from its appearance path; read those concrete boundaries without declaring their scheduling comments guaranteed platform behavior. The lab acceptance report should identify exact fixtures and any executed UI path. Detailed spring tuning, matched geometry across complex trees, gesture arbitration inside custom containers, and assistive-input user testing remain specialist practice. This session supplies the contracts needed to approach that work safely and explain failures.

quiz.question: What does withAnimation do in the disclosure example?

quiz.question: Why keep a drag's current translation in GestureState?
options: It persists a position to disk.
It replaces all committed state.
It is transient and resets when the gesture ends or is cancelled.
quiz.explanation: Render committed position plus transient translation, then commit the final displacement once if required. Accumulating every intermediate translation double-counts movement.

quiz.question: Two text fields use .focused(..., equals: .name). What is the problem?
options: Programmatic focus on .name has an ambiguous target.
Hashable enums cannot be used for focus.
Both controls automatically share one text binding.
quiz.explanation: Focus identity should uniquely name the intended control. Focus bindings do not merge text ownership or choose a predictable target for duplicate enum cases.

exercise.brief: Build a scratch disclosure, a drag with movement limits, and a scrolling two-field editor. Check interrupted input and ways to act without dragging.
steps: Toggle DemoDisclosure repeatedly with reduced motion off and on. Compare its final state and visible content.
Add movement limits to DemoDrag and buttons or accessible actions for essential movement and reset.
Keep list IDs stable. Change content or window size, then scroll with the proxy from the current reader.
Use one optional focus enum with a different case for each field. Add an action that clears focus.
Record cancelled input, repeated actions, keyboard behavior, and VoiceOver checks separately from screenshots.
acceptance: The final disclosure visibility always matches its state after interrupted animation.
Cancelled transient drag input does not accidentally double-commit position.
Essential actions can be completed without performing a drag.
Programmatic scrolling targets the intended current ID after reordering or resizing.
Each focus case names exactly one field, and keyboard dismissal does not clear the draft.
exercise.solution:
The disclosure's Boolean is its source of truth, the value that decides the final content. Repeated taps can interrupt the movement, but the latest value must win. Reduced motion changes the visual policy while keeping that result. For a bounded drag, add temporary translation to the saved position, then clamp the candidate so it stays inside the allowed rectangle. Display that candidate and save it once at successful completion. Reset is an accessible action; add ordinary movement controls when needed. Use the actual container geometry, not UIScreen.main.bounds.

A two-field focus enum has distinct name and note cases. Return from name requests note; Done or an explicit toolbar action assigns nil. Neither mutation should reconstruct the model. For scrolling, observe the event inside ScrollViewReader and use a stable row or bottom-marker ID after the desired content is present. Do not preserve a proxy in an appearance-time closure just to share it widely.

The verification record should show one cancelled drag, one cancelled navigation gesture if implemented, one narrow-window keyboard-visible scroll, and one reduced-motion completion. Directly calling a gesture callback is useful for logic but is not evidence that UIKit/SwiftUI recognizers arbitrate correctly. This solution describes the expected design and scratch observations; it does not claim the client UI was run.
